analysis.one_liner: Helps residents of the 100 most toxic-burdened counties win inspections, funding, and possible bans on new polluting facilities.
analysis.headline: The bill died in committee: Senator Al Gore introduced it in June 1992 with zero cosponsors, and it never received a vote before Congress adjourned in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have ranked every U.S. county by the total weight of toxic chemicals present and singled out the 100 worst as 'Environmental High Impact Areas.' In those counties, the EPA and OSHA would have had to inspect every toxic chemical facility at least every two years, and residents would have been eligible for small grants to hire their own technical experts. A government study would then compare cancer, birth defect, and infant mortality rates in those counties against everywhere else, and if significant harm showed up, the bill would have blocked new toxic facilities from being sited there until health-based levels were met.
analysis.who_benefits: People living in counties with the heaviest toxic chemical burdens — often low-income and minority communities near industrial facilities. They would get regular government inspections of local facilities, up to $50,000 grants to pay for technical help participating in the process, a federal health study of their counties, and — if harm was proven — a moratorium on new toxic facilities and proposed legislation to close reporting loopholes and tax emissions.

how_it_helps.text: The EPA must rank all counties by the total weight of toxic chemicals present over five years and designate the 100 worst as Environmental High Impact Areas, with the list republished at least every five years.
The EPA and the Labor Department must inspect or review every toxic chemical facility in those areas within two years of enactment, and at least every two years after that.

Residents affected by potential toxic releases can get grants of up to $50,000 for technical assistance with inspections and health studies, funded by user fees on the toxic chemical facilities themselves.

The Department of Health and Human Services must report on acute and chronic health impacts — including cancer, birth defects, infant mortality, and respiratory disease — in the high-impact counties compared to other counties.

If the study finds significant adverse health impacts, new toxic chemical facilities cannot be sited or permitted in affected areas unless a need is demonstrated and releases are minimized, and the President must send Congress proposed legislation to remedy the harm.

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of toxic chemical facilities in the 100 designated counties, who would bear user fees to fund community grants, mandatory compliance inspections every two years, a possible moratorium on new siting, and — if harm were documented — possible emission taxes and tighter reporting requirements.

drawbacks.text: The bill's headline remedies are deferred: it first requires studies and reports, and the siting moratorium and legislative fixes only trigger if a later report documents significant harm, meaning no immediate emissions reduction in affected communities.

Ranking counties purely by the total weight of toxic chemicals present — even chemicals contained in barrels or lined landfills — is a blunt measure that may not match actual exposure or health risk in a given community.
Community grants are capped at $50,000, limited to one per county, subject to appropriations, and normally require recipients to cover 20% of the cost themselves unless they show financial need.
A siting moratorium could block facilities a community actually wants or needs, though the bill includes an exception where the need is demonstrated and releases are minimized.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the communities the bill targets, the direct benefits — frequent inspections, funded technical assistance, and a rigorous federal health study — are real but modest, and the strongest tools are conditional on later findings. The bill is more of a data-and-leverage framework than an immediate cleanup. Still, it would have shifted power toward residents of heavily polluted counties at the expense of facility operators' fees and compliance burdens, and its main flaw is slowness, not poor design.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Environment and Public Works Committee, which never acted on it, and it expired when the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.

narrative.text: Senator Albert Gore, Jr. introduced the Environmental Justice Act of 1992 in the Senate on June 3, 1992.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Environment and Public Works, where it stayed; no further action was taken.
The 102nd Congress ended on January 3, 1993, so the bill died without ever reaching the Senate floor.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Toxic chemical facility operators in heavily polluted counties are better off, since they avoided new user fees, mandatory inspections every two years, a potential moratorium on new facilities, and possible emission taxes. Residents of those counties gained nothing from the bill's death.

for.name: Sen. Albert Gore, Jr.
for.role: U.S. Senator from Tennessee; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Environmental Justice Act of 1992 and was its only sponsor.

against.name: Senate Committee on Environment and Public Works
against.what_they_did: Never considered or reported the bill after it was referred on June 3, 1992, keeping it from the Senate floor.

sides.party_line_note: There were no votes and no cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition never showed up in the record; the sole sponsor was a Democrat.

industries.industry: Chemical manufacturers and toxic chemical facility operators
industries.note: The bill would impose user fees on facilities in the 100 designated counties to fund community grants, require a compliance inspection at least every two years, and — if a health study documented harm — block new siting and pave the way for emission taxes and tighter reporting. Its gain from the bill's death is the absence of these costs and restrictions.
Waste facilities under Solid Waste Disposal Act permitting count as toxic chemical facilities, so they would face the same fees, inspections, and potential siting moratorium in designated counties.
